answers.label: Q1(a)
answers.finalAnswer: Where the Wind Goes
answers.solution: A suitable title: **Where the Wind Goes** (or 'The Wind and My Kite'). The poem is about the poet wondering where the wind comes from and where it goes.

answers.label: Q1(b)
answers.finalAnswer: The wind is very strong: if he let go of the string, it would carry his kite away for a day and a night.
answers.solution: The poet thinks the wind is very strong. If he stopped holding the string of his kite, the wind would carry the kite away with it 'for a day and a night'.

answers.label: Q1(c)
answers.finalAnswer: No. Its destination can be found by following the kite, but where it comes from nobody can ever know.
answers.solution: No, there is nothing common between them in the poet's opinion. He believes he can find out where the wind goes by letting his kite fly with it and finding where it lands. But where the wind comes from remains a mystery: 'nobody knows'.

answers.label: Q1(d)
answers.finalAnswer: The wind is very fast: it flies as fast as it can, and he could not keep up with it even if he ran.
answers.solution: The poet thinks the wind is very fast. It is 'flying from somewhere as fast as it can', and he could not keep up with it even if he ran.

answers.label: Q1(e)
answers.finalAnswer: (iii) The poet knows nothing about the wind.
answers.solution: (iii) The poet knows nothing about the wind. He says, 'No one can tell me, nobody knows where the wind comes from, where the wind goes.'

answers.label: Q1(f)
answers.finalAnswer: (iv) Personification
answers.solution: (iv) Personification. In 'It's flying from somewhere, as fast as it can', the wind is described as if it were a living being trying its hardest.

answers.label: Q1(g)
answers.finalAnswer: keep up with
answers.solution: **keep up with** ('I couldn't keep up with it, not if I ran.')

answers.label: Q2(a)
answers.finalAnswer: We have lost our old warm sociability and cannot build a new social life on the European standard.
answers.solution: Our home-life has become joyless because we have lost the old habit of meeting one another informally and warmly, and we do not have the means to build a new social life on the European standard.

answers.label: Q2(b)
answers.finalAnswer: They are no longer filled with friendly gatherings, conversation and laughter; they look empty and deserted.
answers.solution: The rooms and verandahs have lost their charm because people no longer gather there informally. The hum of conversation and the laughter have gone, so they look empty and deserted.

answers.label: Q2(c)
answers.finalAnswer: Today people meet only for business, politics or social duty; in the past they met informally for the pleasure of each other's company.
answers.solution: People of the past met informally and often, simply for the joy of being together, with lively talk and hearty laughter. The present generation meets only on business, for political purposes or as a social duty, never just for the pleasure of meeting one another.

answers.label: Q2(d)
answers.finalAnswer: No longer making opportunities to bring people together out of love for them, and not sharing our homes and hospitality with others.
answers.solution: Social miserliness means being stingy in our social life: we no longer make opportunities to bring people together simply because we love our fellow men, and we do not share our homes and hospitality with others, especially the poor. The author finds nothing uglier than this.

answers.label: Q2(e)
answers.finalAnswer: We should revive warm, informal social gatherings and meet one another out of love, making everyone feel at home.
answers.solution: The author's message is that we should bring back the warm sociability of the past. We should meet one another not only for business but out of love for our fellow men, and make everyone, rich or poor, feel at home. Such fellowship makes home-life joyful.

answers.label: Q3
answers.finalAnswer: Three essays: (a) Our cultural heritage; (b) Co-education; (d) A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
answers.solution:
Topics chosen: (a), (b) and (d).

**(a) Our Cultural Heritage**

India has a cultural heritage that is thousands of years old. It includes our monuments, languages, music, dance, festivals, food and values. The Taj Mahal, the Ajanta caves and the temples of the south show the great skill of our ancestors. Classical dances like Bharatanatyam and Kathak, and the music of the sitar and tabla, are admired all over the world. Festivals such as Diwali, Eid, Christmas and Pongal teach us to live together in harmony. Respect for elders and the belief 'Atithi Devo Bhava' (the guest is like God) are also part of this heritage.

Sadly, many young people are forgetting their roots, and many old monuments are damaged by neglect. It is our duty to learn about our heritage, protect it and pass it on proudly to the next generation.

**(b) Co-education**

Co-education means that boys and girls study together in the same school. It is common in India today.

Co-education has many benefits. Boys and girls learn to respect each other and to work together as equals. Healthy competition makes both groups work harder. Shyness and wrong ideas about the other sex disappear, and children grow up confident. Since boys and girls will work together in offices and in society later, co-education prepares them for real life. It also saves money, because separate schools are not needed.

Some people feel that co-education can distract students. But with good teachers, discipline and proper guidance, this problem can easily be avoided.

On the whole, co-education helps to build a fair and balanced society, where men and women understand and respect each other.

**(d) A Chain is Only as Strong as its Weakest Link**

A chain is made of many links. If even one link is weak, the chain breaks at that point, however strong the other links may be. In the same way, a team, a family or a nation is only as strong as its weakest member.

In a cricket team, if one fielder drops easy catches, the whole team may lose. In the army, every soldier must be fit and alert, because one careless soldier can put the whole unit in danger. A country cannot progress if a large part of its people remain poor and uneducated.

So a good leader does not ignore the weak members. He helps them, trains them and makes them strong. We too should help classmates who are weak in studies. When every link is strong, the whole chain becomes unbreakable.

answers.label: Q4
answers.finalAnswer: Letter to the editor of the New Times on the alarming population rise that slows the nation's development.
answers.solution:
45, Main Market
Pitampura
Delhi
10 December 2019

The Editor
The New Times
Delhi

Subject: Alarming rise in population

Sir,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw attention to the alarming rise in our population in recent years and the harm it is doing to the nation's development.

Our country's population has crossed 130 crore. Every year millions are added, but our land, water and resources stay the same. As a result, there is a shortage of jobs, houses, schools and hospitals. Our cities are overcrowded, our roads are jammed and pollution is increasing. Much of the money meant for development is spent just on meeting basic needs, so progress is slow and poverty remains.

The government must spread awareness about small families, especially in villages, and make education and health care available to all. Every citizen must also understand that a small family is a happy family.

I hope the authorities will take this problem seriously.

Yours faithfully,
Rehan
Pitampura, Delhi

answers.finalAnswer: Precis titled 'Little Acts Reveal Character'.
answers.solution:
**Title: Little Acts Reveal Character**

Just as light shines through tiny holes, small actions reveal a person's character, which is built from good deeds done daily. Our behaviour towards others is a key test of character. Polite conduct towards everyone, whether above, below or equal to us, pleases them because it shows respect, and pleases us even more. Anyone, rich or poor, can learn to be courteous. Gentleness is quieter, yet stronger and more fruitful, than force.

(76 words)

answers.label: Q6
answers.finalAnswer: School magazine article by Gaurav on plastic pollution as a threat to the environment.
answers.solution:
**Plastic Pollution: A Real Threat**
by Gaurav, Class VII, Modern School, Dehradun

Plastic is everywhere in our lives: in bags, bottles, toys, packets and straws. It is cheap, light and useful, but it has become one of the biggest threats to our environment.

Plastic does not rot. A single bag can stay in the soil for hundreds of years. Plastic waste blocks drains and causes flooding in cities. When it is burnt, it releases poisonous gases into the air. Cows and dogs eat plastic bags along with food and die. In the oceans, turtles, fish and birds get trapped in plastic or swallow it by mistake. Tiny bits of plastic have even entered the water we drink and the food we eat.

We can all help. We should carry cloth or jute bags, use steel bottles, say no to straws and plastic cutlery, and put waste in the right dustbins so that it can be recycled.

Let us take a pledge today to make our school and our city free of plastic.

answers.label: Q7
answers.finalAnswer: Story with title about Hari, welcomed home with garlands and a band after winning a gold medal.
answers.solution:
**The Pride of Our Town**

The moment Hari stepped down from the train he was greeted at the platform by the people of his small town. They had gathered there with garlands and a band. Drums were beating, and children were waving flags and shouting his name.

Only two years ago, Hari had been a poor boy who ran barefoot on the dusty roads to deliver milk every morning. The village sports teacher, Mr. Negi, saw how fast he ran and began to train him. There were no proper shoes and no running track, but Hari practised every day before sunrise. Many people laughed at him, but he never gave up.

Last week, Hari had won the gold medal in the 400-metre race at the National Junior Athletics Championship. His photograph was in every newspaper.

Now, as garlands piled up around his neck, Hari saw his mother standing quietly at the back with tears of joy in her eyes. He pushed through the crowd, touched her feet and placed the medal around her neck. Then he turned to Mr. Negi and said, 'This medal belongs to you both.'

The whole platform burst into cheers.

answers.finalAnswer: (a) (ii) Ruined; (b) (ii) Compromise; (c) (i) An anxious suspense; (d) (i) Yield; (e) (i) Small amount of money
answers.solution:
(a) GILDED THE LILY (spoiled something already beautiful by adding too much decoration): (ii) Ruined
(b) SPLIT THE DIFFERENCE (meet halfway between two amounts): (ii) Compromise
(c) TENTER-HOOKS (in anxious suspense): (i) An anxious suspense

Note on (b): 'find a happy medium' also describes a compromise, and option (iv) 'all of these' may be what the setter intended; 'strike a deal' does not mean the same thing, so (ii) is the best single answer.

answers.label: Q13
answers.finalAnswer: (a) Preposition; (b) Noun; (c) Adverb; (d) Adjective; (e) Preposition
answers.solution:
(a) 'past 9 PM': **Preposition** (it relates the time to '9 PM')
(b) 'his past': **Noun** (it follows 'his' and names something)
(c) 'had gone past': **Adverb** (it tells us more about the verb 'gone' and has no object)
(d) 'past experience': **Adjective** (it describes the noun 'experience')
(e) 'walked right past his friend': **Preposition** (it has the object 'his friend')

Note: as printed, the word 'past' is not underlined in (b); it is the only possible word.

answers.label: Q14
answers.finalAnswer: (a) (ii) Cheek by jowl; (b) (ii) Spilled the beans; (c) (ii) Much of muchness; (d) (i) Took him to the cleaners; (e) (i) Come a cropper
answers.solution:
(a) at daggers drawn (bitter enemies), opposite: (ii) Cheek by jowl (very close)
(b) swept under the carpet (hid), opposite: (ii) Spilled the beans (revealed a secret)
(c) like apples and oranges (very different), opposite: (ii) Much of muchness (very alike)
(d) greased his palm (gave him money as a bribe), opposite: (i) Took him to the cleaners (took his money from him)
(e) came off with flying colours (succeeded), opposite: (i) Come a cropper (failed badly)

Note: (d) is the weakest item; none of the options is a clear opposite of bribing, and (i) is the closest reading.

answers.label: Q15
answers.finalAnswer: (a) leaves; (b) are playing; (c) swam; (d) say; (e) will have completed
answers.solution:
(a) The Howrah Express **leaves** at 5 PM. (Simple present for a fixed timetable.)
(b) They **are playing** the guitar now. (Present continuous for an action happening now.)
(c) It has been six years since he **swam** like this. (Simple past after 'since' for a past point.)
(d) If I say something once I **say** it a hundred times. (Simple present for a habit.)
(e) By the end of this month we **will have completed** the work. (Future perfect with 'by'.)

Note: as printed, (a) is missing the word 'at' before '5 PM', and (d) is missing 'a' before 'hundred'. In (d) the sentence seems to be built on the saying 'If I've said it once, I've said it a hundred times'; with 'say' in the first half, 'say' is the matching form.
